title: A Kid Who Loses Everything Isn't Lazy — The Prefrontal Cortex Isn't Done Yet
dek: A 14-year-old boy's prefrontal cortex won't finish developing until 25, so losing things isn't an attitude problem. The real problem: parents whose own executive function is already stretched thin have to build a system the kid can't possibly hold up.
why: This episode has medium information density, but it breaks ‘executive function’ into operable mechanisms: why an alarm is more reliable than memory, why a visual timer beats a phone, why you can't push a kid on something he doesn't care about. Good for parents anxious about the back-to-school season.
who: Parents of middle-schoolers drowning in school emails at back-to-school time, whose kids lose everything and who drop the ball themselves; people doing adolescent psychology or educational consulting.
skip: The sponsor ads at the start and end, the Season 7 format-change notes, and the lawyer disclaimer at the end.

points.h: The prefrontal cortex isn't done until 25, and not at 18 either
points.body: Tori defines executive function as ‘a set of behaviors and processes led by the prefrontal cortex,’ and the brain develops ‘from back to front,’ with the prefrontal cortex the last part to mature, not ‘fully cooked’ until a kid is in their twenties. So a 14-year-old boy still has ten years to grow. She specifically points out: we don't expect any high school graduate to have executive function ‘fully wrapped up’ — an 18-year-old brain just isn't at that developmental level. But a lot of parents think that by 10th, 11th, 12th grade the kid should ‘have it all figured out’ — that expectation itself is wrong.

points.h: Parents have to catch their own guilt first, then talk solutions
points.body: The mom who wrote in said ‘I see myself in him’ and wondered if it was her fault. Tori says before giving advice you have to stop, because for a lot of parents there's a string of scary questions behind this: Did I make him this way? Will this follow him his whole life? What will he be like at 18? She also reminds us to ‘hold two things at once’: for that boy, wearing the wrong T-shirt to the first practice is the end of the world, and that feeling is real; but in the big picture, this is the textbook definition of a ‘natural consequence’ — you didn't know to bring the jersey, so there's no jersey, it feels awful, and then we go back to the drawing board and figure out how to make this happen less often. Not bypassing the discomfort, but turning the discomfort into fuel for building a system.

points.h: The system has to be simple enough to hold, with a safety net
points.body: Tori thinks of a system as ‘a division of labor’: who's responsible for checking Google Classroom, who's responsible for checking the soccer team's app, while keeping a big safety net. If checking notifications is the son's job, the parent should still glance at it regularly to make sure nothing big slips through. Lisa shares her own approach: when her daughter ran cross-country in 10th grade, after getting an email from the coach she'd still yell from the kitchen, ‘Did you get this email?’ and wouldn't let it go until it was confirmed, sometimes just copy-pasting the content into a text to her daughter with a note, ‘Assuming you saw this.’ Tori says this trick is enough for kids without major executive function issues, but a lot of families need a more fixed, more consistent way of checking.

points.h: Don't rely on memory — rely on a 6 p.m. Sunday alarm
points.body: Ideally you'd sit down at 3 p.m. Sunday and go through the coming week, but Tori says this ‘all sounds lovely until there's a soccer game at 2 p.m. Sunday, the 3 o'clock check time has already passed, and it never happened.’ So the second layer is the safety net: set a repeating alarm on your phone for 6 p.m. every Sunday, called ‘weekly check.’ If you already did it at 3, turn this one off; if you didn't do it or something else knocked it out, this reminder tells you ‘before the week takes off, you need to do this.’ Lisa presses: so it's two slots on the calendar, 3 p.m. for theoretically doing it, 6 p.m. to confirm it actually got done, but 6 p.m. doesn't rely on memory — Tori says ‘I can't remember anything at 6 p.m. on a Sunday.’

points.h: There is no organization fairy, only lists and reminders
points.body: Tori and Lisa spent years counseling at a school and found some kids believe ‘the organization fairy will sprinkle some magic on me someday.’ Both of them react: no, buddy, there is no organization fairy, she's not coming. The kids who look organized aren't organized because they remember everything — they're organized because they have lists, a planner, to-do lists, reminders. Tori says this gap is ‘what we forget to fill in for our kids’ — it's not a switch that flips on by itself. And the more distractions there are (an after-school job, caring for younger siblings, managing a chronic illness), the more you need a good, simple system to support executive function that's ‘still under construction.’

points.h: Three free tools: alarms, email snooze, visual timers
points.body: Tori starts with the things that cost nothing. First, the alarm function on your phone — she set six alarms this morning herself, one of them to confirm the carpool for her son's afternoon soccer game, because ‘our kids don't drive yet.’ She does a little check before taking the phone away at night, asking herself: ‘What is there today that I'm very likely to forget?’ Second, the email ‘snooze’ function, made specifically for those ‘mark this date, it's an October thing’ emails — you can't think about October now, so let it pop back up in three weeks instead of relying on memory to go dig it up. Third, a visual timer, aimed at ‘time blindness’: for people with a poor sense of how much time has passed or how long something takes, seeing time elapse visually is very helpful.

points.h: The tool that helps a kid focus is the very thing that distracts him
points.body: Lisa quotes Angela Duckworth: we generally don't put ice cream next to the broccoli. She asks: if I'm relying on the phone to keep my kid on track, but the phone is exactly the thing that derails him most, what do I do? Tori first admits adults are the same — you pick up the phone to set an alarm, then get sucked into email, reply to the first text, and then ‘I've spent my whole life asking: what did I come in here to do?’ She says asking kids to do this with an underdeveloped prefrontal cortex puts them at a disadvantage to begin with. Her solution is low-tech: a Time Timer, the kind with a red pie slice, battery-powered, with nothing on it that can distract you. Also, say your purpose out loud before picking up the phone — ‘I'm picking up the phone to set this alarm’ — to prime yourself and remind yourself there's only one task on this device.

points.h: You can't push a kid on something he doesn't care about
points.body: Tori explains why executive function is ‘uneven’: bandwidth is limited, impulse control is limited, and it drops when depleted, so the more important things in a day get attention first — work, picking up the kids — not returning the library books. But the hardest question is: what if this 14-year-old doesn't care about school at all and doesn't see any risk? Tori says first find what he does care about — for example, playing soccer has a minimum GPA requirement, and you can't miss too many practices. Tie the requirements to what he actually cares about: if you want to keep playing soccer, here are the things we want to see happen, and here are the structures we'll build around you. The key is that this conversation can't happen in the heat of the moment when ‘he forgot about tomorrow's test’ — it has to wait until everyone has calmed down.

points.h: When to get an evaluation: does it bleed into what he cares about
points.body: The letter asks: how do you know if it's normal ‘still pulling it together’ or time to refer for an evaluation? Tori says collect feedback from several places. The school has already raised executive function concerns in middle school, and after the school year starts the parent should bring it up proactively at the October parent-teacher conference. The advantage of high school is having different teachers, not just one teacher's opinion — some who teach subjects he cares about, some who teach subjects he doesn't. Then look at two things: whether these relatively simple systems can't even touch the problem, and whether the problem is starting to bleed into the places he really cares about, like soccer, or hanging out with friends. If so, it may be time to get more information and evaluate for an underlying cause like ADHD.

terms.def: A set of abilities led by the prefrontal cortex: planning, organizing, inhibiting impulses, remembering what you need to do.
A poor sense of how much time has passed or how long something takes, common in people with ADHD and executive function difficulties.
Observing your own thinking process, like asking yourself ‘what am I very likely to forget today.’
Not intervening in advance, letting the kid bear the consequences of the behavior itself — e.g., no jersey means no jersey to wear.

quotes.text: So even parents with fantastic executive functioning skills struggle during this time of year. It's hard because it's hard. It's not hard because you're doing it wrong.
This is the last part of the brain to fully develop. It will not be fully cooked until this kid is in his mid-20s.
It's not that they're remembering all of these things. It's that they have checklists and they have planners and they have to-do lists and they have reminders.
So the fact that we expect adults to do this, and now we're expecting kids to do it with an underdeveloped prefrontal cortex. It's kind of stacked against them.
And if we think about executive functioning, it's like impulse control. We don't have an unlimited amount of this. And it goes down as it is taxed.

And this is a conversation that we have not in the heat of the moment when they've forgotten to study for the test that's tomorrow. This is a later conversation when everybody has cooled down a little bit.
The bottom line is we have to work with the kid we got. We get to work with the kid we've got.
